bullets: How a centre-seeking force, the gravitation law and a 24-hour period turn circular motion into orbits: circular motion and gravitation
slides.heading: JC H2 physics — mechanics: circular motion and gravitation
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we build mechanics from the ground up - a centre-seeking push that holds every circular path, the size of that force, gravity holding the Moon, a satellite that hovers over one spot - and the trap of the fling-off force at the end.

bullets: Explain why circular motion needs a centripetal force directed to the centre, and compute it with F = mv^2/r
Use gravitation F = GMm/r^2 as the centripetal force for orbits, and state the conditions for a geostationary orbit with period 24 hours
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the trap that a centrifugal force flings you outward.

bullets: A car turns sharply and you slide across the seat - it feels as if something flings you outward
Is there really an outward force, or does your body simply keep going straight while the car turns under you?
slides.heading: In a sharp turn, what pushes you sideways?
slides.notes: Ask the class to commit to a guess before any definitions: is there an outward fling force in a turn, yes or no? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the trap scene of the lesson settles this question completely.

bullets: Every object in circular motion is pulled or pushed toward the centre: without that centre-seeking force it would fly off on a tangent
For orbits, gravity itself supplies the centripetal force, and the period fixes the orbit radius
slides.heading: One idea, five scenes: centre-seeking force, its size, gravity, sync, trap
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: circular motion is not a new kind of motion needing a new outward force - it is straight-line motion constantly bent inward by one real, centre-seeking force.

bullets: A satellite stays on its circular path only because a force keeps pulling it towards the centre
The force arrow always points at the centre, no matter where the satellite is on its orbit
slides.heading: Circular motion needs a centre-seeking push
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the satellite move from the right to the top to the left of the orbit - the red force arrow swings round with it, always pointing at the planet in the centre.

bullets: Centripetal acceleration is a = v^2/r: spin twice as fast and it quadruples; double the radius and it halves
Multiply by the mass for the force: F = mv^2/r
slides.heading: How big is the centre-seeking force
slides.notes: Work the two scalings in order: first double v and watch the force arrow grow to four times, then double r and watch it halve. Say: the v-squared is the dangerous one - small speed increases demand much bigger forces.

bullets: For the Moon, gravity itself supplies the centripetal force: F = GMm/r^2
Every orbit is a continuous fall towards the centre that keeps missing the Earth
slides.heading: Gravity holds the Moon in orbit
slides.notes: Link the two formulas explicitly: set GMm/r^2 equal to mv^2/r and the Moon's speed follows. Say: the same pull that gives you weight on a bathroom scale is the pull holding the Moon in its circle.

bullets: A geostationary satellite orbits above the equator with a period of exactly 24 hours, turning at the same rate as the Earth below
From the ground it seems to hang motionless in the sky - perfect for weather and broadcast satellites
slides.heading: Geostationary orbits hover over one spot
slides.notes: Walk the sync condition slowly: same angular speed as the Earth, above the equator, in the same direction. The synced dot stays over its home point while the drifter falls behind - period alone is not enough without the equator and direction.

bullets: The imagined outward arrow does not exist: there is no centrifugal fling in a sharp turn
Your body keeps going straight on the tangent while the seat pushes you inward - the inward push is the real force
slides.heading: Misconception: the fling-off force
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: being thrown sideways feels like an outward push, but the only horizontal force on you in the turn points inward, from the seat and the door, toward the centre.

bullets: Step 1: a 0.50 kg ball on a 1.2 m string at 6.0 m/s needs F = mv^2/r = 0.50 x 36 / 1.2 = 15 N toward the centre
Step 2: doubling the speed to 12 m/s quadruples the force to 60 N - the v-squared scaling in action
slides.heading: Worked example: centripetal force and a gravitation check
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: always compute mv^2/r first, then ask what supplies that force - here the string tension, for the Moon gravity.

bullets: A 1200 kg car rounds a bend of radius 50 m at 15 m/s. Find the centripetal force needed and state what supplies it
Careful - a classmate says: A centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn. Explain to them what really happens to a passenger in the turn
slides.heading: Your turn: compute, then correct
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on F = mv^2/r = 1200 x 225 / 50 = 5400 N first, then on the exact sentence they used to talk their classmate out of the claim: A centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn.

bullets: On your own: a satellite doubles its orbital speed at the same radius. By what factor does the required centripetal force change, and why?
Watch out for the trap one last time: A centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn. Say what force, if any, acts outward on a passenger in a sharp turn
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for the factor of four from v-squared in your first answer and one clear sentence about the missing outward force in your second. Anyone repeating the claim A centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn. needs the trap scene again.
